title: Methods
intro: Braising, poaching, sautéing, roasting and the other ways heat meets food in the classical kitchen. Each method is a set of choices about fat, liquid and temperature, made for a reason.

entries.title: Sauté and the shallow fry
entries.summary: Sautéing cooks small or thin pieces fast in a little hot fat, tossed or turned; shallow frying uses more fat and a coating. Heat, a dry surface and room in the pan decide whether food browns or steams.
entries.guest: Sautéed means cooked quickly in a hot pan, so the fish stays moist and flaky with a light golden edge.

paras: Sauter is French for to jump. A sauté is small or thin pieces of food cooked fast in a little hot fat in a wide, shallow pan, tossed or turned so every surface meets the metal: fish fillets, shrimp, tender cuts, mushrooms. The heat is high and the cooking takes minutes. It is often the first pan method a new cook learns, because it teaches what every pan method depends on: heat, a dry surface and room.

Shallow frying is its close cousin. The fat is deeper, about 1 cm (1/2 inch), a third of the way up the food, and the food usually wears a coating: seasoned flour, or flour, egg and breadcrumbs. It suits cutlets, crab cakes and soft-shell crab, which want a crisp jacket and are turned once rather than tossed.

The order never changes: the pan hot before the fat, the fat hot before the food, the food dry and never crowded. Heat the empty pan, add a thin film of oil or clarified butter and wait until it shimmers; whole butter burns at this heat because of its milk solids. Pat the food dry and season it just before it goes in. Lay it in one layer with space between the pieces. Crowd the pan and its heat drops, juice leaks out and the food stews grey, because a wet surface cannot climb past 100°C (212°F) and so cannot brown.

For a fish fillet, dry it well and, if the dish wants a crust, dredge it in seasoned flour and shake off every loose speck. Lay it presentation side down first, the side the guest will see, or skin side down for crisp skin, pressing it flat for a moment so it does not curl. Leave it alone: it releases from the pan once the crust has formed. Turn it once, lower the heat and finish gently. A thin fillet takes two or three minutes in all; a thick one is browned on the stove and finished in the oven.

For a shallow fry, heat the fat to about 170 to 180°C (338 to 356°F), when a crumb dropped in sizzles at once. Lay the coated food in away from you so the fat cannot splash back, fry until golden underneath, turn once and drain on a rack, where the crust stays crisp.

Three words describe one pan at three heats. To sweat is to cook gently in a little fat over low heat, often with a pinch of salt or a lid, until vegetables are soft and translucent with no colour: the start of a soup, a rice pilaf or a Creole sauce built on the trinity. To sauté is medium-high heat and movement, for a light golden colour. To sear is the hottest pan and no movement at all, for a deep crust on a steak or a scallop. The classic pans are the sloping-sided sauteuse, built for tossing, and the straight-sided sautoir, which also holds a sauce.

Food that sticks went into a pan not hot enough, was wet, or was moved before its crust let go. Food that greys and weeps was crowded. A coating that slides off was not patted dry or was turned too often. A dark outside with a raw centre means the piece was too thick for the heat: lower the flame or finish it in the oven.

The children’s dinner at Brennan’s offers Sautéed Gulf Fish with Potato and Green Beans, the day’s Gulf fish cooked quickly in a hot pan. The children’s menu is read from the restaurant’s web card rather than the server guide, so confirm the plate and its set price on the live card. At breakfast and lunch, the Pecan Gulf Fish is likely pan-roasted or sautéed to order, and the kitchen confirms which. The fish changes with the catch: learn today’s fish and how it is cooked at lineup.

Say soh-TAY, and give the guest the plain picture: cooked quickly in a hot pan. Is a sautéed fish fried? Not deep-fried: it is cooked in a little fat in a hot pan, where frying uses far more fat and usually a batter or crumb. Never guess the fish; it is the day’s catch. Questions about what it is dusted in, or the fat it is cooked in, go to the kitchen.

cards.front: What does the French word sauter mean, and what does a sauté describe?

questions.q: Which order sets up a sauté correctly?

distractors: Cold pan, fat and food together, then heat
Hot pan, then the food, then fat poured over
Warm fat, wet food, the pan filled to the edge
questions.why: Each step keeps the surface hot: a hot pan heats the fat, hot fat browns at once, and dry, uncrowded food never cools it.

questions.q: Fish cooked in a crowded pan comes out pale and wet. Why?

distractors: The fat was too hot and scorched the crust at once
The fish was dredged in flour first
The pan was heated for too long beforehand
questions.why: Too much food cools the pan and releases juice; a wet surface stays near the boiling point of water and cannot brown.

It makes a coating slide off
It turns the fish grey
questions.why: Whole butter carries milk solids that blacken at sauté heat; oil or clarified butter takes the heat, and whole butter goes in late.

questions.q: When sautéing a skinless fish fillet, which side goes down first?
questions.answer: The presentation side, the side the guest sees
distractors: The side that will rest face down on the plate

Neither: it is turned constantly
questions.why: The first side meets the hottest pan and takes the cleanest, most even crust, so it is the side that faces up on the plate.

questions.why: A sweat is low heat and no colour, a sauté is medium-high and golden, and a sear is maximum heat for a deep crust.

Add more cold fat
Press it flat with a spatula
questions.why: The oven’s surrounding heat cooks the centre through gently while the crust, already made, stops darkening.

entries.title: Pan-roast and poêlé
entries.summary: Two ways to roast in a pan. Pan-roasting sears on the stove, finishes in a hot oven and bastes with butter on its return; poêlé roasts tender meat in butter on vegetables in a covered pot, uncovered at the end to colour.
entries.guest: Pan-roasted means seared in a hot pan for a golden crust, then finished in the oven, so it stays juicy inside.

paras: Pan-roasting is how a restaurant cooks a thick piece to order. It is seared hard in an ovenproof pan on the stove, the same pan goes into a hot oven, and on its return to the stove it is basted with foaming butter. The crust comes from the stove, the even cooking from the oven, and one pan does both. It suits fillets, chops and steaks too thick to cook through by searing alone.

Poêler (pwah-LAY) is the older, gentler cousin. A tender bird or a fine cut is set on a bed of matignon: carrot, onion and celery cut small, with raw ham, thyme and bay, stewed soft in butter. It is buttered, covered and cooked in a moderate oven, then uncovered near the end to colour. The classical books treat it as a roast made under a lid.

Heat the oven to about 200 to 220°C (392 to 428°F). Dry and season the meat or fish and sear it in a little oil in an ovenproof pan until the presentation side is deep golden. Turn it and put the pan straight into the oven: a few minutes for a thick fish fillet, longer for a chicken breast or a chop, judged by a probe against the chef’s chart. Bring the pan back to the stove holding the handle with a dry cloth, because it is now as hot as the oven.

To baste, arroser in the French kitchen, add a knob of butter, a sprig of thyme and a crushed clove of garlic, tilt the pan so the butter pools, and as it foams spoon it over the meat for a minute. The foam carries the herbs onto the crust, browns it further and gives it a nutty flavour. Stop before the butter turns from hazelnut to burnt, then lift the meat out to rest.

To poêler a chicken, stew the matignon in butter in a heavy pot just large enough for the bird. Season the bird, set it on the vegetables, pour melted butter over, cover and cook in a moderate oven, about 160 to 180°C (320 to 356°F), basting every 10 to 15 minutes. For the last 15 to 20 minutes take off the lid so the skin browns. A chicken is done at 74°C (165°F) in the thickest part of the thigh; duck, pigeon and fillet of beef are served pink, checked with a probe.

The vegetables are the start of the sauce, never a bed to throw away. Lift the bird out to rest, pour a little veal stock into the pot over the matignon, butter and juices, simmer it a few minutes, then strain and skim off the fat. Served in its pot, the dish is called en cocotte or en casserole.
A chef also reads the timing: each pan-roast holds an ovenproof pan and a place in the oven for up to about 15 minutes, so the station fires it first and builds the garnish around it.

Poêlé sits between a roast and a braise. Like a roast, it uses tender meat and fat and stops when the meat is just cooked; like a braise, it is covered and sits on vegetables. The difference is liquid. A braise is half covered in stock or wine and cooks tough meat for hours; a poêlé has little or none beyond the butter and the meat’s own juices. A roast is open to dry heat throughout. That is why poêlé suits tender poultry, game birds and fine cuts such as a fillet of beef, which butter and vegetables keep moist.

A thick grey band under the crust means the outside cooked far ahead of the centre: a long sear in a pan that was not hot enough, or too long in a hot oven. Dry meat stayed in too long, and bitter basting butter met too fierce a flame.

On a modern menu, pan-roasted marks a thick piece cooked to order: a chicken breast with its skin, a pork chop, a thick fillet of fish. Give the guest the plain picture: seared for a golden crust, then finished in the oven. Poêlé seldom appears by name; a chicken en cocotte is the same method, a bird roasted in butter in a covered pot on vegetables, often brought to the table in its pot. At Brennan’s the Pecan Gulf Fish is likely pan-roasted or sautéed to order: learn the day’s fish and its cooking at lineup.

cards.front: What are the stages of a pan-roast?
cards.back: Sear in an ovenproof pan on the stove, finish in a hot oven in the same pan, then baste with foaming butter on its return.

cards.front: Why finish a thick cut in the oven rather than on the stove?
cards.back: Surrounding heat cooks it through evenly; left on the stove, the crust would burn before the centre was done.

cards.back: The handle is as hot as the oven. Grip it only with a dry cloth, and mark it, often with a dusting of flour, so nobody grabs it bare; keep every cloth clear of the flame.

cards.front: What does arroser mean, and how is it done?
cards.back: To baste: tilt the pan and spoon foaming butter, thyme and garlic over the meat as it finishes, browning the crust and adding flavour.

cards.front: What is a poêlé?
cards.back: A tender bird or cut roasted in butter in a covered pot on a bed of matignon, basted, then uncovered at the end to colour.

cards.front: What is the matignon under a poêlé?
cards.back: Carrot, onion and celery cut small, with raw ham, thyme and bay, stewed in butter: the bed a poêlé cooks on and the start of its sauce.

cards.front: Why does poêlé suit tender poultry and fine cuts rather than tough ones?

cards.front: How do you describe a pan-roasted dish to a guest?

To flame with a splash of spirit
To deglaze with wine

A thick layer of coarse salt
Stock poured halfway up the sides of the meat

Ox cheeks trimmed of sinew
An old boiling hen

questions.answer: So the skin can brown

So the bird can rest in the pot
So the vegetables can soften further
questions.why: Under the lid the bird cooks moist but the skin stays pale; uncovered and basted for the last minutes, it takes colour.

questions.q: What chiefly separates a poêlé from a braise?
questions.answer: Little or no liquid beyond the butter
distractors: A poêlé is never covered at any stage
A braise is made with no vegetables at all
A poêlé is cooked on the stove top only
questions.why: Both are covered and sit on vegetables, but a braise is half covered in liquid for tough meat, while a poêlé cooks tender meat in butter.

questions.q: How is a poêlé’s sauce made?

questions.why: The butter, juices and matignon left in the pot hold the flavour; a little veal stock lifts them, and straining and skimming finish it.

entries.title: Braise and daube
entries.summary: Braising sears a tough, hard-working cut, then cooks it slowly, covered, with wine or stock partway up, until its collagen melts into gelatine and the liquid becomes its sauce. A daube is Provence’s red wine braise, marinated first.
entries.guest: Braised means browned, then cooked slowly in a covered pot with wine or stock for hours, so it is fork-tender and the cooking liquid becomes its sauce.

paras: To braise is to brown a large piece of meat hard, then cook it slowly in a covered pot with liquid coming partway up its sides. It is the method for tough, hard-working cuts: short rib, chuck, shank and cheek. These muscles are laced with collagen, the connective tissue that makes them chewy. Held for hours in moist heat below the boil, collagen melts into gelatine from about 70°C (158°F), which keeps the fibres moist, makes the meat spoon-tender and thickens the liquid into a glossy sauce. The gelatine is the reward, and the reason a braise cannot be hurried.

Season and dry the meat, then sear it in a little oil in a heavy pot until deep brown on every side: that crust, and the browned bits it leaves on the pot, the fond, flavour the finished sauce. Lift the meat out, pour off most of the fat and soften onion, carrot, celery and garlic in what remains. Pour in the wine, scrape up the fond and reduce it by about half to cook off its raw edge, then add stock.

Return the meat. The liquid comes a third to halfway up, never over it: the exposed top cooks in the steam trapped under the lid while the rest simmers, and takes a glaze if the lid comes off for the last half hour and it is basted.

Add a bouquet garni, a tied bundle of herbs, bring it just to a simmer, cover and move it to a low oven of about 150 to 160°C (302 to 320°F), or keep it at a lazy simmer on the stove, the surface barely moving. Short rib and chuck take roughly 2 1/2 to 3 1/2 hours, shank and cheek often longer. It is done when a fork slides in and out with no pull, not at a time on a clock.

Finishing turns the liquid into a sauce. Lift the meat out, strain the liquid, let it settle and skim off the fat, or chill it overnight and lift the set fat away. Reduce it until it coats a spoon; if it needs more body, thicken it with beurre manié (butter and flour kneaded together) or mount it with cold butter. Season, then warm the meat through in its sauce.

A daube (DOHB) is the red wine braise of Provence. Beef in large pieces is marinated overnight in red wine with garlic, herbs and often a strip of orange peel, then cooked slowly in a daubière, a pot-bellied earthenware pot. Boeuf bourguignon and coq au vin are Burgundy’s red wine braises of beef and of cockerel, with lardons, mushrooms and small onions. A white braise skips the browning and uses pale stock, for veal, sweetbreads or vegetables such as leeks and celery.

New Orleans Creole cooks kept the daube, and daube glacée, the braised beef set cold in its own jelly, is a dish of the Creole Christmas table. Grillades, beef or veal rounds braised in a brown roux gravy with the trinity and tomato, are the Creole braise and have their own entry.

Tough meat has not cooked long enough: collagen needs hours. Dry, stringy meat was boiled rather than simmered, or cooked far past tender. A pale, thin sauce lacked a good sear or was never reduced. A sour, winey edge means the wine went in with the stock unreduced. A greasy sauce was not skimmed, and a bitter one came from a fond burnt black in the sear.

At Brennan’s the braise is the short rib débris (DAY-bree) on the Eggs Owen, at breakfast and lunch. It is braised the classic way: short rib seared hard, the vegetables sweated, the pan deglazed with red wine and reduced, then stock added and the pot cooked in a low oven for about three hours, until a fork turns the meat; the liquid is skimmed and reduced and the meat pulled back into it. Confirm the kitchen’s own steps and timing at lineup. Débris is Louisiana French for scraps.

Describe a braise as slow-cooked: browned, then cooked for hours in a covered pot until fork-tender, its own liquid the sauce. Call the débris slow-cooked beef that falls apart into its own gravy. The menu does not say Eggs Owen is named for Owen Brennan, so confirm at lineup before telling that story. Ingredient questions go to the kitchen.

cards.front: What does it mean to braise?
cards.back: To sear meat, then cook it slowly, covered, with liquid partway up, until its collagen melts into gelatine and the liquid becomes its sauce.

cards.front: Which cuts are made for braising, and why?
cards.back: Short rib, chuck, shank and cheek: hard-working muscles full of collagen, which melts into gelatine with long, moist heat.

cards.front: Why does a braise take hours?
cards.back: Collagen turns to gelatine slowly, from about 70°C (158°F); only time makes a tough cut tender and the sauce glossy.

cards.front: How far up the meat should braising liquid come?
cards.back: A third to halfway, never over it: the base simmers and the top cooks in the trapped steam. Covered completely and cut small, it is a stew.

cards.front: What heat does a braise want?
cards.back: A lazy simmer, the surface barely moving, or a low oven of about 150 to 160°C (302 to 320°F). A hard boil makes dry, stringy meat.

cards.front: Why sear the meat before braising?

cards.front: What is a Provençal daube?

entries.title: Poaching, shallow and deep
entries.summary: Poaching cooks food gently in liquid held below the simmer, so eggs, fish and chicken stay moist and nothing browns. Deep poaching submerges the food; shallow poaching half covers fish on shallots and turns the liquor into the sauce.
entries.guest: Poached means cooked gently in hot liquid kept below a simmer, so it stays soft and moist. Our poached eggs come with soft, runny yolks.

paras: To poach is to cook food in liquid kept hot but below the simmer: the surface trembles and steams, and only an odd bubble rises. That gentle heat sets proteins slowly, so they do not tighten and squeeze out their juice, which is why poaching suits delicate foods: eggs, fish, chicken breast, fruit. Nothing browns, so the flavour stays clean, and the liquid, water, stock, wine or milk, flavours the food. Learn to read the water: a poach barely shivers, a simmer sends up lazy bubbles at about 85 to 95°C (185 to 203°F), and a boil rolls at 100°C (212°F).

Deep poaching covers the food completely in liquid held at about 70 to 85°C (158 to 185°F): a whole salmon, a chicken, a thick fillet, pears in syrup. Start large pieces in cool or warm liquid so the outside does not overcook before the centre is done; lower small pieces into liquid already hot. The liquid is often a court-bouillon, an aromatic poaching liquid with its own entry.

Shallow poaching is the classical way with fillets of sole, trout or other white fish. Butter a shallow pan, scatter it with chopped shallot, lay the seasoned fillets on top and pour in fish stock and white wine to come halfway up. Cover with a circle of buttered paper, a cartouche, bring it to a bare simmer on the stove, then finish in a moderate oven until the flesh turns opaque. The liquor left behind, the cuisson, is reduced hard and finished with cream or butter: the cooking liquid becomes the sauce.

The poached egg comes first for most cooks. Use the freshest eggs, whose thick white holds together. Bring water at least 8 cm (3 inches) deep to a bare shiver, with a splash of white vinegar if you like, about 15 ml (1 tbsp) to 1 litre (about 1 quart), to help the white set. Crack each egg into a cup and slide it in close to the surface. After about 3 minutes the white is set and the yolk flows. Lift it with a slotted spoon, blot it on a cloth and trim any ragged edges.

For a busy brunch, kitchens poach ahead. Each egg goes from the pan straight into iced water to stop the cooking and is held cold for the time the chef sets. At service it is reheated in hot water at about 70°C (158°F) for about a minute, until warm through but still runny, then blotted dry.

Fish à la nage, swimming, is fish poached in an aromatic court-bouillon and served in a shallow bowl in some of its liquor. Sole Véronique (vay-ro-NEEK) is shallow-poached sole in a creamy white wine sauce with peeled green grapes, glazed under the salamander; the story credits Escoffier, and the tellings vary. Our Redfish Véronique keeps the name and the grapes, pickled with hibiscus, with a preserved lemon beurre blanc; the menu does not say how the redfish is cooked, so ask the kitchen before describing it.

A wispy, ragged egg was stale or went into water boiling too hard. A rubbery white and a firm yolk cooked too long or too hot. Fish that falls apart dry was poached at a boil. A thin, flat sauce from a shallow poach was not reduced far enough before the butter or cream went in, and an egg that tastes sharp met too much vinegar.

At Brennan’s the poached egg is the heart of the Eggs Hussarde and the Eggs Sardou. On the Hussarde, poached eggs sit on our own English muffins and coffee-cured Canadian bacon, with two sauces, hollandaise and marchand de vin, a red wine sauce. On the Sardou, they sit on crispy artichokes and Parmesan creamed spinach under Choron, a béarnaise with tomato. The eggs come soft, the white set and the yolk running, and the house guide asks servers to check with the kitchen before promising a guest firmer eggs.

To a guest, poached means cooked gently in hot water kept below a simmer, so the white is tender and the yolk runs into the sauce when the guest cuts in. A guest who wants a firmer yolk hears that you will ask the kitchen, never a promise.

entries.title: Eggs to order and the omelette
entries.say: As it reads: eggs to order and the omelette.
entries.summary: Fried, scrambled, boiled and rolled: the everyday eggs of a breakfast kitchen, each a matter of heat, fat and timing. The cook makes exactly what the ticket asks, and the French omelette is the test every cook is set.
entries.guest: How do you like your egg? I will write it exactly: over easy, sunny side up or scrambled. Our Crab & Corn Omelette is filled with Louisiana lump crab and roasted sweet corn.

paras: Eggs to order are the short list a breakfast cook makes all morning: fried, scrambled, boiled and the omelette. Each is the same egg given a different heat, fat and time, so a cook learns them by name and a server writes them word for word.

Two facts sit under all of them. Egg white begins to set at about 62°C (144°F); the yolk thickens at about 65°C (149°F) and sets by about 70°C (158°F), so a few degrees decide whether it runs, turns jammy or sets. And eggs keep cooking off the heat, so the cook stops early and lets carryover finish.

Fried eggs: crack each egg into a small dish first, to keep the yolk whole, then slide it into butter foaming over a medium-low flame. Sunny side up is never turned, its yolk left runny. Basted means a lid on the pan, or spoonfuls of hot butter, so a thin veil of white sets over the yolk. Turned eggs are flipped gently: over easy for 20 to 30 seconds, the yolk runny; over medium for about a minute, the yolk jammy; over hard until the yolk is set.

Scrambled eggs come two ways. The French way, oeufs brouillés, is eggs beaten with salt and stirred without stopping in butter over low heat until they thicken into small, creamy curds, with cold butter or cream stirred in to stop the cooking. The American way is quicker, over medium heat, with larger, firmer curds. Either way they leave the heat while still slightly wet, because carryover finishes them on the plate.

Boiled eggs are lowered from the fridge into water at a steady simmer, so the timing is exact and they peel more easily; a simmer, not a hard boil, keeps them from cracking. For a large egg, about 6 minutes gives a set white and a runny yolk, a minute or two more a jammy one, and 10 to 11 minutes a set yolk. Then into iced water, which stops the cooking, eases peeling and prevents the grey-green ring that forms when sulphur from an overcooked white meets the iron in the yolk.

The French omelette is the cook's test. Beat 3 eggs with a pinch of salt until no streaks of white remain. Heat 15 g (1 tbsp) of butter in a 20 cm (8 inch) pan over brisk heat until it foams, never browns, then pour in the eggs and stir fast with a fork while shaking the pan, so they set in small, soft curds. After about 30 seconds, while the top is still moist, baveuse in French, roll it away from the handle and turn it out seam down: pale, smooth and soft at the centre.
3 eggs and 15 g (1 tbsp) of butter in a 20 cm (8 inch) pan for a French omelette; about 6 minutes for a soft-boiled large egg, 10 to 11 for hard; 20 to 30 seconds on the second side for over easy.

The American omelette is set flat, not stirred: the cook lifts the edges so raw egg runs under, lays the filling over one half, folds it and slides it out, firmer and lightly golden. The filling goes in warm, cooked and drained, because a cold one holds the eggs on the heat. Both need an egg pan, kept for eggs alone, never scoured and sized to the eggs, so they set neither thin and rubbery nor thick and raw.

Most egg faults are heat faults: lacy brown edges, rubbery whites, a watery scramble, a browned omelette. A broken yolk comes from cracking straight into the pan or flipping roughly; a grey ring from too long in the pot or no iced water after.

Brennan's breakfast carries a soft-boiled egg on the Eggs Owen, its yolk running into the short rib débris, and a sunny-side-up egg on the Duck Confit Waffle and, from Vital Farms, on the Creole-Spiced Hanger Steak. The Crab & Corn Omelette holds Louisiana lump crab and roasted sweet corn, with miso butter, lemon, basil and a Marcona almond gremolata. Egg Any Style is one egg, made as the ticket reads.

Ask the style and the doneness and write them exactly. Describe the omelette by its filling until lineup says whether it is rolled or folded, and which styles the kitchen offers. A firmer egg on a signature plate, or a question about runny yolks, means a check with the kitchen, not a promise.

cards.front: What is a sunny-side-up egg?

cards.front: How do over easy, over medium and over hard differ?
cards.back: All three are fried and turned. Over easy keeps the yolk runny, over medium leaves it jammy, over hard cooks it right through: different eggs, so the ticket names the style exactly.

cards.front: Why do scrambled eggs come off the heat before they look done?

entries.title: Boil, blanch and steam
entries.say: As it reads: boil, blanch and steam.
entries.summary: Three water methods every cook uses daily: a rolling boil in salted water for pasta and green vegetables, a brief blanch and an iced refresh to set colour and prepare for service, and steam for gentle, moist cooking that keeps shape.
entries.guest: Blanched means cooked briefly in boiling water and cooled fast, which keeps vegetables bright and crisp; steamed means cooked over the water, never in it, so the food stays moist.

paras: Boiling, blanching and steaming are the plainest ways heat meets food: through water, or the steam rising from it. Water at a full boil, 100°C (212°F) at sea level, gets no hotter however hard the flame, so nothing browns and the food tastes of itself. The skill is in the details: how much water and salt, how long, and what happens when the food comes out.

Boiling cooks food through in the water. Blanching, blanchir in French, uses the same boiling water for a brief plunge only. Steaming holds the food above the water, in its vapour. The gentler poach and the simmer have their own entry.

Boiling means a full rolling boil: big bubbles that keep breaking even when the food goes in and the pot is stirred. Use plenty of water, about 1 litre (about 1 quart) for every 100 g (3.5 oz) of pasta or vegetables, so it comes back to the boil quickly, and salt it well, about 10 g to the litre, so the food is seasoned all through. Green vegetables boiled this way and served plainly with butter are called à l'anglaise, in the English style.

Blanching is a brief plunge in boiling water: seconds for spinach and herbs, 2 to 3 minutes for green beans. It sets the colour of green vegetables, loosens skins, tames bitterness and part-cooks food to be finished in moments during service. Refreshing, rafraîchir, follows at once: into iced water to stop the cooking and hold the green, only until cold, then drained and dried well, because clinging water thins the butter or sauce it meets later.

Monder is blanching to peel. Score a small cross in the base of a tomato, plunge it into boiling water for 10 to 15 seconds, until the skin curls at the cross, then refresh it and slip the skin off; peeled, seeded and diced, it becomes a concassée. Peaches are skinned the same way after about 20 to 30 seconds, and almonds after about a minute, when the skins slip off between the fingers. Bones and meat for a white stock are blanched from cold: brought up to the boil, boiled a few minutes, then drained and rinsed of their grey scum, so the stock starts clear.

Steaming cooks food in the vapour above boiling water: a basket or perforated tray over a pan with a close lid, the food never touching the water. Steam gives up a great deal of heat as it condenses on the food, so steaming is quick yet gentle, and fish, vegetables and dumplings keep their shape and flavour instead of losing them to the water. A combi oven, combining steam with fan heat, steams whole trays at once; a parcel of leaf or paper, the method of en papillote, steams food in its own juices.

Green vegetables turn olive and dull when cooked too long, covered, or with acid. Heat releases acids from the vegetable's own cells, and acid turns bright green chlorophyll into an olive-brown pigment. A large pot of fast-boiling water cooks them quickly, and an open pot lets some of those acids escape in the steam, so cook them fast and uncovered, and add lemon or vinegar only at the end. Bicarbonate of soda (baking soda) keeps the green but turns vegetables mushy and soapy, so the classical kitchen relies on speed.

Creamed spinach, under the Eggs Sardou and as a breakfast and lunch side, is classically spinach blanched, plunged into iced water and squeezed hard before the cream goes in, so it stays rich rather than watery; how the kitchen builds ours, and whether the two are one preparation, are questions for the kitchen. Buttered noodles, on the children's dinner, are classically pasta boiled in well-salted water until just tender, then tossed with butter and grated cheese; the menu names neither the shape nor the cheese, so the kitchen has the answer.

Steam burns harder than boiling water, because it gives up its heat as it condenses on skin. Tilt a lid away from you as you lift it, stand back as a combi oven door opens, and lower food into boiling water rather than dropping it.

These words reach the dining room on menus and in questions. Blanched means briefly boiled and cooled; steamed, cooked over water, never in it; à l'anglaise, plainly boiled and buttered. A request for vegetables steamed rather than buttered goes to the kitchen, not a promise.

entries.title: En papillote
entries.summary: Food sealed in a parcel of paper, foil or leaf and baked, so it steams in its own juices with its aromatics. The parcel puffs as the steam builds, and the burst of scent when it is opened is the point.
entries.guest: En papillote means in paper: the fish is sealed in a parcel and baked, so it steams in its own juices. Ours is wrapped in banana leaf, with tomato, olives and crab.

paras: En papillote, said ahn pah-pee-YOHT, means in paper. The food, most often fish, is sealed in a parcel with aromatics, butter or oil and a splash of liquid, then baked. Inside, the liquid and the fish's own juices turn to steam, so the food cooks gently and moistly, and every bit of aroma stays trapped until the parcel is cut open. It is steaming in a closed package, done in the oven.

It suits delicate fillets of white fish and salmon, scallops, chicken breast and young vegetables: foods that cook quickly and would dry out under fiercer heat. Because nothing escapes, the juices left in the parcel become the sauce.

Cut a large heart of baking parchment, about 30 to 35 cm (12 to 14 inches) across, and brush it with butter or oil. On one half lay a bed of aromatics cut fine enough to cook in the time the fish takes: a julienne, thin matchsticks, of leek, carrot and fennel, with sliced shallot, herbs and lemon. Set the seasoned fillet on top, add a knob of butter or a spoon of oil and 15 to 30 ml (1 to 2 tbsp) of white wine or stock. Fold the paper over, then crimp the edges in small, tight, overlapping folds all the way round and twist the tip, so no steam can escape.

Bake the parcels on a tray in a hot oven, about 200°C (392°F). Time by thickness: a fillet 2.5 cm (1 inch) thick needs roughly 12 to 15 minutes, a thinner one less. The parcel puffs as the steam builds, which shows the inside is at full steam. Fish is done when it flakes and reaches 63°C (145°F) at its thickest point, which a probe through the paper of a test parcel can confirm. Serve at once, before the parcel sags.

The wrapper changes the dish. Parchment puffs high and browns a little at the edges, and it makes the best show at the table. Foil seals tighter and copes with a grill, but it neither puffs nor browns, and long contact with acid such as tomato or lemon can pit it. Banana leaf, softened first over a flame or in hot water so it folds without splitting, adds a faint grassy, tea-like aroma; corn husks, fig leaves and vine leaves each lend their own scent. A crust of salt or of dough works on the same idea, sealing a whole fish or joint as it bakes.

A parcel that leaks lets the steam out, so the fish dries and the paper never puffs: fold tighter and overlap every crimp. Hard vegetables beside soft fish mean the garnish was cut too thick; cut it fine or blanch it first. A pool of thin liquid means too much wine or watery vegetables. Because the parcel hides the fish, the commonest fault is overcooking, so cut fillets to an even thickness and time them.

At Brennan's the Gulf Fish en Papillote wraps the day's Gulf fish in banana leaf instead of paper, with tomato, Castelvetrano olives, Louisiana crab, sorghum and Marcona almonds, so it steams in its own juices. The fish changes with the catch, so learn it at lineup. New Orleans knows the method from Antoine's pompano, which has its own entry.

Opening the parcel is the moment. Whether it is opened at the table, and by whom, is a lineup question; when it is, the parcel is cut across and folded back away from the guest, so the steam rises away from faces and the aroma reaches the table first. Warn the guest that the steam is hot. Name the fish, describe the leaf and the garnish, and send any question about the crab or the almonds to the kitchen.

entries.title: Confit
entries.summary: From the French confire, to preserve: meat salted, then cooked slowly submerged in fat until it is meltingly tender, and kept under that fat. Duck leg is the classic; garlic, tomato and fish are cooked the same gentle way in oil.
entries.guest: Our duck leg is confit, kohn-FEE: cured with salt, then cooked slowly in duck fat until tender, and crisped before it comes to you so the skin crackles.

paras: Confit, said kohn-FEE, comes from the French confire, to preserve. It is the larder method of Gascony and the south-west of France, from the days before refrigeration: duck or goose legs salted, cooked slowly while submerged in their own fat, then stored in crocks sealed under that fat for months. The salt draws out moisture and seasons the meat; the fat shuts out air.

What began as preserving became a reason in itself. Cooked gently below the simmer, the tough, sinewy leg turns meltingly tender as its connective tissue softens, yet it stays moist, because the fat around it holds the heat steady and lets no water boil away. The meat does not turn greasy: little of the fat enters it. In French pastry the same word means candied, fruit cooked slowly in sugar syrup, as in fruits confits.

Duck leg confit starts with a cure. Rub the legs with about 30 g of salt for each 1 kg (2.2 lb) of duck, about 3 per cent of their weight, with crushed garlic, thyme, bay and black pepper, and leave them covered in the fridge overnight, 8 to 24 hours. Rinse off the salt and dry the legs well; left too long in the cure, the meat turns hard and over-salted.

Lay the legs snugly in a pan, cover them completely with melted duck fat, and cook them in a low oven or over the lowest flame, the fat barely moving, with only a few small bubbles rising from the meat, about 85 to 95°C (185 to 203°F). After about 2.5 to 3 hours, sometimes more, a skewer slides into the thigh with no resistance and the meat begins to pull from the bone. Hotter fat fries the meat into stringy toughness instead.

To keep it, let the legs cool in the fat, pressed down so every piece is covered, and chill them; the fat seals out air. The dark jelly that settles beneath is the meat's own juice: good in a sauce, but it spoils sooner than fat, so for a long keep it is lifted away. To serve, lift a leg from the fat, wipe it and crisp it skin side down in a pan over medium heat, or in a hot oven, until the skin shatters, handling it gently, because the meat is now fragile.

Confit reaches well beyond duck. Goose, pork and duck gizzards, gésiers, are cured and cooked the same way in south-western France. Garlic cloves cooked slowly in oil until soft and sweet are garlic confit; tomatoes baked slowly in olive oil with garlic and herbs are tomato confit; fish such as salmon or tuna can be cooked very gently in oil until just set. Onion confit, cooked down slowly with sugar and vinegar, borrows the sugar sense of the word.

A confit in oil does not keep the way a cured duck leg under fat once did. Garlic or vegetables held in oil at room temperature can grow the botulism toxin, so garlic and tomato confit are kept chilled and used within days, under the kitchen's own dating rules. In a modern kitchen duck confit lives in the fridge too.

At Brennan's the Rohan duck leg on the Duck Confit Waffle is confit, crisped and served on a cornbread and chive waffle. Rohan is a special Mallard and Pekin cross raised for D'Artagnan in New York State, not a breed. Menus often describe confit as cooked in its own fat, though kitchens use pooled duck fat, so describe the method in general and promise no house cure or cooking times.

Say confit plainly: duck leg cured, cooked slowly in duck fat until tender, then crisped, so the skin crackles and the meat falls from the bone. Guests often expect it to be greasy; it is not, because the meat cooks in the fat without soaking it up. Questions about the waffle and what goes into it go to the kitchen.

entries.title: Roast and baste
entries.say: As it reads: roast and baste.
entries.summary: Roasting cooks meat or poultry in the dry heat of an oven: high heat to brown the outside, lower heat to cook it through. Basting adds colour and flavour, and resting lets carryover heat finish the centre.
entries.guest: Roasted means cooked in the dry heat of the oven, browned outside and rested so it stays juicy. Our Chateaubriand is roasted whole for two, so it takes longer than a steak.

paras: Roasting is cooking by dry heat in an oven. Hot air and the heat thrown off the oven walls brown the outside of a joint, a large piece of meat, or a whole bird, while heat travels slowly inward to cook the centre. No liquid goes in the pan, which is what separates a roast from a braise. The browning is the Maillard reaction, the chemistry behind a seared crust, and it is where most of a roast's flavour comes from. In the classical brigade the rôtisseur ran the roasts, and often the grill and fryer too.

Season ahead. Salt a large joint or a whole bird the day before, about 10 g (0.35 oz) of fine salt for each 1 kg (2.2 lb), and leave it uncovered in the fridge: the salt seasons deeper as it is drawn back into the meat, and the dry surface browns better. Take the chill off for 30 minutes to an hour before cooking, within the kitchen's time rules. Tie a joint into an even shape so it cooks at one rate, and set it on a rack or a bed of bones and vegetables so hot air reaches underneath.

The classic roast starts hot, about 220°C (428°F), for 15 to 20 minutes to brown, then drops to about 160°C (320°F) to cook through gently. Searing first in a hot pan does the same browning on the stove. Many cooks now reverse the order: roast low, about 120°C (248°F), until the centre is nearly there, then brown hard at the end. This reverse sear gives meat that is pink almost to the edge, with only a thin grey band under the crust.

Baste as it roasts. Every 15 to 20 minutes, tip the pan and spoon its hot fat and juices over the meat; the French word is arroser, to water. Basting colours and flavours the surface and keeps lean skin from drying, but it does not push juice into the meat, and every opening of the door costs the oven heat, so baste quickly.

Carryover is heat still travelling inward after the roast leaves the oven. The outside is far hotter than the centre, so the centre keeps climbing: a beef tenderloin taken out at 52°C (126°F) for medium-rare rises to about 55 to 57°C (131 to 135°F) as it rests. That is why a roast comes out before it reaches its target. Beef served below 63°C (145°F), the figure food safety charts give for whole cuts, is covered by the consumer advisory on undercooked meat.

Rest the roast on a rack in a warm place, loosely covered, for 10 to 20 minutes for a large joint and about 5 for a duck breast, then carve across the grain. Resting lets the juices settle and thicken a little, so they stay in the slice instead of flooding the board.

Judge doneness with a probe thermometer pushed into the thickest part, away from bone, and check more than one spot. A whole chicken is read in the thickest part of the thigh and must reach 74°C (165°F). Touch helps on small cuts: raw meat is soft and firms as it cooks, so an experienced cook can press a steak and know it. A roast is too big to judge that way; the probe decides.

At Brennan's the Roasted Chateaubriand is the centre cut of a Creekstone Farms tenderloin, roasted whole for two so it stays juicy; its sauce and plate are taught in their own entry. The Roasted Rohan Duck Breast, the fourth course of the dinner tasting, is roasted so the skin renders and the meat stays rosy; a duck breast is classically scored, rendered skin down, finished in the oven, rested and sliced across the grain, and the kitchen's own steps are confirmed at lineup.

The kitchen and the ticket speak of doneness in words, rare, medium-rare, medium, medium-well and well done, each a band on the chef's chart, taught in Cooking terms on the ticket. Write the guest's word exactly, and for the Chateaubriand ask once for the whole table, since one roast serves both. Tell the table at the order that a whole roast takes longer than a steak, and ask at lineup where it is carved tonight. The duck is usually served medium-rare to medium: confirm the kitchen's standard and tonight's garnish at lineup before you describe it.

entries.title: Grill and salamander
entries.say: As it reads: grill and salamander.
entries.summary: Grilling cooks food on bars over heat from below, marking it and flavouring it with smoke from the dripping fat. The salamander is the professional kitchen's overhead grill (broiler): fierce heat from above for finishing, glazing and gratins.
entries.guest: Grilled means cooked on bars over a flame, for dark marks and a smoky edge. A gratin's golden top comes from a moment under fierce heat from above.

paras: Grilling is cooking on metal bars over heat from below: glowing charcoal, gas burners or burning wood. The heat reaches the food two ways, as radiant heat from the fire and by direct contact with the hot bars, which brand dark lines into the surface. Fat and juices drip onto the heat, smoke and sometimes flare, and that smoke is part of the flavour. It is fast, fierce heat, so it suits tender, fairly thin food: steaks, chops, fish, shrimp, vegetables and split chicken.

The salamander turns the fire upside down. It is a gas or electric element above a rack that can be raised or lowered, usually mounted over the range. It gives fierce heat from above for seconds or a minute or two: to brown a gratin, glaze a sauce, melt cheese or finish a dish that is already cooked. The name comes from an old kitchen tool, an iron plate on a long handle heated in the fire and held over a dish to brown it, itself named for the creature that legend said could live in flames.

Build zones. On a charcoal grill, bank the coals deep on one side and thin on the other; on gas, set one burner high and one low. The hot zone, about 260°C (500°F) at the bars, marks and sears; the cooler zone, around 175°C (347°F), finishes thick pieces gently, lid down, without burning the outside. A cook can read the heat with a hand held about 12 cm (5 inches) above the bars: two or three seconds before it must come away means hot, five or six means medium.

Mark and turn. Scrape the bars clean and heat them well, dry the food and brush it lightly with oil, then lay it down and leave it: it sticks until a crust forms, then lets go. For crosshatched marks, the French quadrillage, give the piece a quarter turn on the same side after a minute or two, then turn it over and finish. Move anything that flares to the cooler zone rather than drowning the flames.

Under the salamander, heat the dish through first, in the oven or on the stove, because the salamander only colours: a cold gratin burns on top and stays cold beneath. Then set the rack close and watch every second. A Mornay gratin, vegetables or pasta under a béchamel enriched with cheese, bubbles and browns in a minute or two. A sabayon, egg yolks whisked with wine and sugar to a warm foam and spooned over fruit, takes colour in seconds and catches if you turn away. Oysters Rockefeller, on the half shell under a rich green topping, need fierce top heat so the topping bubbles before the oysters overcook.

Chargrilled oysters are the modern New Orleans classic of the grill. At Drago's in Metairie, Tommy Cvitanovich began cooking oysters on the half shell over a hot grill in 1993, under garlic butter, herbs and grated Parmesan and Romano. The butter bubbles and flares, the edges of the oysters curl, and French bread on the side mops up the butter. Drago's calls them charbroiled oysters, and the dish has spread across the city.

For a guest, grilled means bars and a flame: a smoky edge and dark marks. A gratin or a glazed sauce has met the salamander for its golden top. Blackening is neither: it is a spiced crust cooked in a very hot iron pan, taught in its own entry. And an American grilled cheese sandwich is usually toasted in a pan or on a flat griddle, whatever its name says.

British English says grill for both: food goes on the grill, over the heat, or under the grill, beneath it. An American kitchen keeps grill for heat from below and gives the overhead grill (broiler) its own name. Professional kitchens on both sides of the Atlantic call their version the salamander.

entries.title: Smoking, hot and cold
entries.summary: Smoking flavours food with the smoke of smouldering wood. Hot smoking cooks as it flavours, as with andouille and tasso; cold smoking flavours without cooking and always follows a cure. Today smoke is mostly a seasoning.
entries.guest: Our Smoked Cauliflower is smoked for a deep, savoury flavour, then brightened with preserved lemon and a moderate warmth from harissa.

paras: Smoke is what wood gives off when it smoulders, burning slowly with too little air to flame. Heated wood breaks down into hundreds of compounds: some give the smoky, spicy aroma, others react on the surface of the food to give a mahogany colour, and some slow the growth of bacteria and the spoiling of fat. Smoke works on the surface, so a dry, slightly tacky skin, the pellicle, takes it best.

For most of history smoke was a preserver, working with salt and drying to keep meat and fish through lean months. Refrigeration took over that job, and smoke today is chiefly a flavour, but the old order stands: salt first, then smoke.

Hot smoking cooks as it smokes. The food sits in a closed smoker or smokehouse over smouldering wood, at a heat high enough to cook it through, slowly. Andouille, tasso and the smoked sausage of south Louisiana are hot smoked, each cured or seasoned first; so are hot-smoked salmon and trout, which flake when done. Bacon is smoked warm too, but it is still cooked before it is eaten. Rules for hot-smoked fish commonly ask for the centre to be held at 63°C (145°F) or more for at least 30 minutes.

Cold smoking flavours without cooking. The smoke is made apart from the food and cooled before it reaches it, and the chamber is kept below about 32°C (90°F), the ceiling smoked seafood guidelines set, so the flesh does not cook: smoked salmon stays silky, cheese stays whole, and some hams take smoke for days. That warmth is no barrier to bacteria, so cold smoking always follows a cure: salmon is salted, often with sugar, rinsed and air-dried to a pellicle before the smoke.

Choose the wood. Hardwoods give clean smoke: hickory strong and bacon-like; pecan, a kind of hickory, milder and sweeter; oak steady and medium; fruitwoods such as apple and cherry gentle and sweet. Resinous softwoods like pine and spruce give a bitter, sooty smoke and are never used. The wood should be dry and seasoned and the smoke thin and pale blue; thick white smoke from a smothered fire coats food with acrid soot.

Smoke at the pass is a seasoning, not a preserver. A smoking gun burns a pinch of wood chips and blows cool smoke through a tube under a glass cloche, over a plate, a cocktail or a container of liquid, for a few seconds to a few minutes. Liquids, purées and dressings take smoke quickly, and a little goes a long way.

In south Louisiana the smokehouse and the boucherie belong together. A boucherie is a communal hog butchering, Cajun and Creole alike, born before refrigeration and still held in rural communities, where families and neighbours work together to turn a whole hog into food: boudin, cracklins, hogshead cheese, andouille and more. In those days, meat that could not be eaten fresh was salted, made into sausage and smoked to keep, which is why the two are remembered together in rural south Louisiana.

At Brennan's smoke turns up as a seasoning across the menus: the smoked tomato water poured last over the Creole Tomato Tostada, the smoked oyster dressing of the Creole Caesar, the smoked potato pavé beside the breakfast hanger steak, and the Smoked Cauliflower side at dinner, finished with preserved lemon and harissa. How each one is smoked is the kitchen's detail.

Tell guests where the smoke is before it surprises them. The Creole Caesar's dressing is made with smoked oysters: mention it to every guest, flag it on the ticket and take any shellfish question to the kitchen. Describe smoke as a gentle, savoury note rather than barbecue, and leave the method to the chef.

cards.front: What does smoke come from, and why does the fire not flame?
cards.back: Wood smouldering with too little air to flame; heated slowly, it breaks down into compounds that colour, flavour and help preserve the food.

cards.front: Where does smoke flavour food, and what helps it take?
cards.back: On the surface. A dry, slightly tacky skin called the pellicle takes smoke evenly and well.

cards.front: What is hot smoking?
cards.back: Smoking at a heat that cooks the food through as it flavours it: andouille, tasso and hot-smoked fish that flakes.

cards.front: What centre temperature and time do rules commonly set for hot-smoked fish?
cards.back: At least 63°C (145°F) at the centre, held there for at least 30 minutes.

cards.front: What is cold smoking, and what is it used for?
cards.back: Smoking with the chamber below about 32°C (90°F), so the food takes flavour without cooking: smoked salmon, cheese and some hams.

cards.front: Why does cold smoking always follow a cure?
cards.back: Cold smoke does not cook, and its warmth suits bacteria, so the salt does the protecting and the smoke adds flavour.

cards.front: Which woods give good smoke, and which are never used?
cards.back: Hardwoods such as hickory, pecan, oak, apple and cherry; never resinous softwoods like pine, which give a bitter, sooty smoke.

cards.front: What should good smoke look like?
cards.back: Thin and pale blue. Thick white smoke from a smothered fire coats food with acrid soot.

cards.front: What does a smoking gun do at the pass?
cards.back: Blows cool smoke under a cloche or into a container for seconds or minutes: a seasoning for a plate, a liquid or a cocktail, never a preserver.

cards.front: What is a boucherie?

entries.title: Frying and the fry station
entries.summary: Deep frying cooks food submerged in clean oil at about 170 to 190°C (338 to 374°F): surface water flashes to steam, the coating sets crisp, and the inside cooks gently in its own moisture.
entries.guest: Popcorn shrimp are bite-size Louisiana shrimp, fried golden and crunchy, with a tangy Crystal hot sauce gastrique, a sweet and sour sauce. Any coating or fryer question, I take to the kitchen.

paras: Deep frying is cooking food fully submerged in hot oil, usually about 170 to 190°C (338 to 374°F). The moment food goes in, the water at its surface boils into steam: that is the furious bubbling. Steam pushing outward keeps most of the oil out while the surface dries and browns into a crust, and inside, the food cooks gently in its own moisture. Get the heat right and fried food is crisp and light; get it wrong and it is greasy or burnt.

Oil that is too cool lets the bubbling slow before the crust sets, and the food soaks up fat. Oil that is too hot browns the outside before the inside cooks, and breaks down faster. Frying in a pan with less fat is shallow frying, taught with the sauté.

Coat it. Most fried food wears a coating that browns into the crust and protects what is inside. The standard breading, à l'anglaise in the classical kitchen (the same phrase also names plainly boiled vegetables), runs flour, egg wash and crumbs: flour dries the surface so the egg clings, and egg glues on the crumbs. Keep one hand for the dry and one for the wet. Louisiana often fries its seafood in a seasoned cornmeal dredge, often after a dip in egg, milk or buttermilk, and batter coats okra and onion rings. Let a breaded piece rest a few minutes so the coating sets.

Fry it. Fill the fryer to its line and heat the oil: about 175°C (347°F) suits most breaded seafood and vegetables, 180 to 190°C (356 to 374°F) small pieces and the second fry of French fries, and about 160°C (320°F) the first, blanching fry of potatoes. Fill the basket no more than half, lower it gently, and fry in small batches: every load drops the oil's heat, and an overloaded basket drops it so far that the food stews in fat. Let the oil recover between batches.

Drain and season. Lift the basket, shake it over the oil, and turn the food onto a rack, never onto paper, where it sits in its own steam and softens. Salt it at once, while the surface oil still holds the salt, and send it straight away: fried food is at its crispest in its first few minutes.

Care for the oil. Skim crumbs between batches, because they burn, darken the oil and flavour the next batch. Filter it at least daily, top it up with fresh oil, and keep salt and water away from it: salt speeds its breakdown, and water makes hot oil spit violently. Fresh oil is pale and smells clean. Change it when it turns dark, smells acrid or fishy, foams and will not settle, or smokes at its normal heat.

Shared oil carries what was fried in it. Shrimp, fish and anything coated in wheat flour or crumbs leave their proteins in the oil, and frying does not destroy them, so food cooked in shared oil can carry traces of what went before. Many kitchens give seafood its own fryer for flavour as well as for that reason, but no server can promise how tonight's fryers are set up: questions about shellfish, coatings, shared fryers and oil always go to the kitchen.

The fryer also burns. Lower food in gently and away from you, and never fill past the line. If the oil catches fire, never use water, which flashes to steam and throws burning oil out of the fryer: turn off the heat, smother it with a lid or the kitchen's class K extinguisher, made for cooking-oil fires, and call the chef.

At Brennan's the fryer works across the menus. The popcorn shrimp at the Roost are bite-size Louisiana shrimp fried golden, with a Crystal gastrique. The artichokes on the Eggs Sardou are cooked tender, then coated and fried crisp. The poussin is a Cornish hen brined in sweet tea, coated and fried before its mustard cream. Brabant potatoes are classically cubed, blanched or par-fried, fried golden and tossed in butter, garlic and parsley, with the house finish and fryer confirmed at lineup; good French fries are usually fried twice, and how the kitchen fries ours is a lineup question.
Fried food waits for no one: run it the moment it is up. Describe it by its crunch and by what is inside, and send every question about coatings, shared fryers or the oil to the kitchen, every time.

entries.title: Deglaze and the pan sauce
entries.say: As it reads: deglaze, pan sauce.
entries.summary: A pan sauce is made in minutes in the pan a piece of meat or fish was seared in: the browned juices are lifted with wine or stock, reduced, enriched and finished, so nothing the searing made goes to waste.
entries.guest: A pan sauce is made from the browned juices left in the pan, with shallot, wine and stock. Our Poussin à la Moutarde carries its cousin, a tangy, rich mustard cream sauce.

paras: To deglaze, déglacer in French, is to pour liquid into a hot pan after searing and scrape up the browned film stuck to its base. American kitchens call that film the fond; French cooks usually call it the sucs, and to them fond chiefly means a base, as in a stock. It is the meat's browned juice, and it dissolves readily, so the pan that cooked the steak becomes the start of its sauce.
A pan sauce is the quickest sauce in the classical kitchen: made to order, in the same pan, while the meat rests. It turns a seared piece into a finished dish.

Sear in a stainless or carbon steel pan; non-stick will not build a fond. Lift the meat out to rest and look at the pan: chestnut to mahogany is right, but black is burnt and bitter, so start again in a clean pan. Pour off all but about 15 ml (1 tbsp) of fat, lower the heat and sweat a finely chopped shallot for a minute, soft and without colour.

Deglaze: pour in the wine, stock or spirit and scrape hard with a flat wooden spatula as it bubbles; the fond lifts within seconds. Wine is the usual choice, because its acid and alcohol draw out flavours that water leaves behind. Reduce it almost dry, au sec, so its raw taste cooks away. A spirit such as brandy goes in off the flame; lighting it is taught with flambé.

Add stock, or stock and cream, and reduce again to nappe, when the sauce coats the back of a spoon. Tip in the meat's resting juices. Off the heat, swirl in cold butter a piece at a time until the sauce turns glossy; why it works is taught with monter au beurre. Season and serve at once.

For two portions: one shallot, about 30 g (1 oz); 120 ml (1/2 cup) of wine reduced to a spoonful; 180 to 240 ml (3/4 to 1 cup) of stock reduced by half; and 30 g (1 oz) of cold butter. That gives about 120 ml (1/2 cup) of sauce. Use unsalted stock and season at the end, because reduction concentrates salt along with flavour.

Change the liquid and the finish and the method gives a family. White wine, shallot and chicken stock suit chicken, veal and fish; red wine and brown stock, mounted with butter, suit steak and duck; cream reduced in the pan makes a cream sauce.

The mustard cream of poulet à la moutarde, the Burgundian bistro chicken, is the model of the cream branch: shallot softened in butter, white wine reduced, cream simmered to nappe, and Dijon mustard stirred in off the heat. Boiled, mustard loses its bite and can turn bitter, so it goes in last and the sauce is not boiled again.

Hence the rule: cream sauces may boil; butter-finished sauces must not. Heavy cream, at 36 per cent fat or more, holds its fat in protected globules and can be boiled hard to reduce it. Light cream, half-and-half and milk curdle, especially with acid in the pan. A butter-mounted sauce breaks at the boil, so the butter goes in last, off the heat.

Bitter: the fond burnt black, or garlic browned too far; start again in a clean pan. Sharp and raw: the wine was not reduced before the stock. Thin: reduce it longer. Sticky: loosen it with stock. Greasy: the fat was not poured off, or the butter boiled. Salty: a salted stock reduced too far; add unsalted stock or a little cream.

At Brennan's the Poussin à la Moutarde carries a mustard cream sauce in the Burgundian bistro tradition, where shallot is softened in butter, white wine reduced, cream simmered and mustard stirred in off the heat so it keeps its bite; how tonight's sauce is built is the chef's detail. The hen is brined in sweet tea and fried, and comes with turnips and shallots: a crisp Southern bird under a French bistro sauce.

Describe the mustard cream as tangy and rich, a French bistro sauce over a crisp Southern bird. The poussin is a whole small bird and may have bones, so say so. Questions about the cream, the butter or the fried coating go to the service note and the kitchen.

entries.title: Monter au beurre
entries.summary: To mount a sauce with butter: cold butter swirled or whisked into a hot sauce, off the boil, at the last moment, for gloss, body and a rounder taste. Simple to do and easy to undo, because a sauce that reboils breaks.
entries.guest: A sauce finished with butter has a little cold butter swirled in just before it comes to you, which gives it its shine and a softer, rounder taste.

paras: Monter au beurre means to mount with butter: cold butter swirled or whisked into a hot sauce, off the boil, just before it goes to the plate. Monter is French for to go up or to mount, and kitchens use it for building anything up. Butter is about four-fifths fat, the rest mostly water with a little milk protein. Swirled in cold and in pieces, it does not simply melt but breaks into fine droplets held in the sauce's water: a light emulsion.

It gives gloss, a little body, a rounder taste that softens the edge of wine and acid, and richness from a small amount. It is the last touch on a great many brown sauces and pan sauces, and the difference between a dull sauce and one that shines at the pass.

Cut unsalted butter, straight from the fridge, into dice of about 1 to 2 cm (1/2 to 3/4 inch). Bring the sauce to the right body first, since butter thickens it only by a shade. Take the pan off the heat so it stops bubbling. Add a few pieces and swirl or whisk gently until they have almost gone, then add more. Keep the sauce moving, hot but below the simmer, roughly 70 to 80°C (158 to 176°F). Taste, season and send it.

Mount at the last moment. A mounted sauce waits only briefly, warm but off direct heat, and goes out within minutes, never longer than the chef's own standard allows. Never reboil it: the fat droplets run together, and the sauce thins, dulls and floats a slick of oil. A sauce built on a stock rich in gelatine mounts readily and holds longer, because gelatine thickens the water around the droplets and helps keep them apart.

A dependable measure is 30 to 60 g (1 to 2 oz) of cold butter for each 240 ml (1 cup) of sauce, an eighth to a quarter of its weight. Less gives shine without richness; much more makes a butter sauce that tastes of little else and breaks at the first knock.

Three butter preparations are easily confused. Mounting finishes a sauce that already exists: the sauce is the body and a little butter the polish. In a beurre blanc, butter is most of the sauce, whisked into a few spoonfuls of reduced wine, vinegar and shallot. A beurre monté is butter emulsified into a little boiling water, a neutral butter for poaching, glazing and holding food moist at the pass. Each has its own entry.

On the stove, a cook mounts a red wine jus, a light sauce of meat juices and wine, just before plating. A deglazed pan sauce is mounted once it reaches nappe, thick enough to coat a spoon. A classical marchand de vin, shallot and red wine reduced and then simmered with demi-glace, a rich brown sauce, is commonly finished with butter. Whether a house sauce such as Brennan's marchand de vin is finished this way is the kitchen's to say. A cream sauce often needs little or none.

Greasy beads or a ring of oil: too hot, or boiled after mounting. Off the heat, whisk in a spoonful of cold water or cold stock, which can pull a lightly broken sauce back; a fully split one is skimmed, brought back to nappe and mounted afresh. Dull and thin: the butter went in soft or all at once. Greasy however long you whisk: too little gelatine in the stock. Set at the edges: held too cool, so warm it gently, never to the boil.

Escoffier's Guide Culinaire, first published in 1903, finishes sauce after sauce with butter added off the fire. Later, the nouvelle cuisine of the 1960s and 1970s turned away from heavy flour-thickened sauces in favour of lighter reductions, and a reduction finished with a little butter remains a familiar restaurant sauce.

Guests seldom hear the French; a menu may say finished with butter, or simply a glossy jus. Describe the sauce, not the technique: a red wine sauce with a silky finish. Send the plate quickly, because a mounted sauce dulls as it waits. A butter finish changes the answer to a guest's question about butter or milk, so that question goes to the kitchen.

entries.title: Flambé
entries.summary: Flambé means flamed: spirit added to a hot pan and lit, so its vapour burns in a short burst of flame. It burns off some alcohol, never all, adds aroma and a touch of caramel, and gives the dining room a show.
entries.guest: Flambéed means flamed: the spirit is lit in the pan and burns for a few moments. The flame takes some of the alcohol, but not all of it.

paras: Flamber is French for to flame, and a dish served flambé has had spirit poured into a hot pan and lit. What burns is not the liquid but the alcohol vapour rising from it, which is why the flame dances above the pan and dies on its own once the vapour runs short, usually in well under a minute.

It burns off some of the alcohol, never all, and much stays in the sauce. The heat of the flame caramelises a little sugar on the surface and leaves the spirit's aroma softer and rounder than it was raw, a real but modest change. Much of the point is theatre, so much flambé is done in the dining room.

Strength matters. Spirits of around 40 per cent alcohol, such as brandy, cognac, dark rum and many orange liqueurs, light readily, especially when warm. Wine and fortified wine, at roughly 12 to 20 per cent, rarely catch in an ordinary pan. Overproof spirits, well above 50 per cent, flare high and fast and have no place on a busy line.

In the kitchen, measure the spirit into a small jug first, about 30 to 60 ml (2 to 4 tbsp) for a sauce for two; poured from the bottle near a flame, fire can travel back up the neck. Pull the pan off the flame and pour in the spirit. Return it and tilt the far edge towards the gas flame to light the vapour, or use a long match on induction. Stand back, a lid within reach to smother it, and let the flame burn out. In a bright room the flame can be almost invisible, so treat the pan as lit until you are sure it has died, and turn the burner off before you step away.

The classics: steak au poivre, a pepper-crusted steak whose pan is often flamed with cognac and finished with cream; steak Diane, with shallot, mustard and cognac, long a tableside favourite; and the flamed desserts, crêpes Suzette with orange liqueur, cherries jubilee and Bananas Foster, each with its own entry.

A brandy and green peppercorn pan sauce shows the method at the stove. Sear and rest the steaks, pour off the fat, and sweat shallot with drained green peppercorns, the soft unripe berries kept in brine. Take the pan off the heat, add about 60 ml (1/4 cup) of brandy from a measure, light it and let it burn out. Add brown stock and reduce by half, add cream and simmer to nappe, then finish with cold butter off the heat.

Will not light: the spirit is too weak, too cold or too little, or the pan has cooled. Warm the pan briefly and tilt again; never add more spirit to a pan that may be alight. Flares too high: too much spirit, an overproof bottle, or spirit poured in over the flame; cover it with the lid. Harsh and boozy: the sauce was not reduced after the flame died, so simmer it longer. Bitter: the sugar or the fond was too dark beforehand.

Cherries jubilee is generally credited to Escoffier, for one of Queen Victoria's jubilees, most often said to be that of 1897; his version was served with warmed kirsch lit at the table, and no ice cream. In New Orleans the flame stayed in the dining room: Bananas Foster was created at Brennan's in 1951, while it was still Owen Brennan's Vieux Carré on Bourbon Street.

At Brennan's two desserts are flamed at the table on a guéridon, the tableside cart: the World Famous Bananas Foster, with rum, and the Cherries Jubilee, tart black cherries in a Luxardo sauce over housemade vanilla ice cream. The house's tableside steps go beyond the kitchen method; they are learned word for word and taught in Flambé safety at the table. Who performs the flambé is a lineup question for the manager, and a new server never lights a pan before sign-off. The Jubilee was not on the dessert menu of 3 October 2026: confirm with a manager before offering it.

Say flahm-BAY, and flahm-BAYD for flambéed. Guests often ask whether the alcohol burns off: not all of it, and much stays in the sauce. For a guest who avoids alcohol, the guide steers to the Lemon Tart or the Pineapple Tarte Tatin. Which rum and spirit the kitchen uses are questions for the chef.
